title: Greedy: Jump Game II (Fewest Jumps)
oneLiner: The fewest jumps to the last index: treat each jump as a BFS level and grow the next level as far as it can go.
keyTakeaway: Indexes reachable in exactly k jumps form a contiguous block, so BFS levels are just ranges. Scan left to right keeping currentEnd (the edge of the block you can reach with the jumps taken so far) and farthest (the edge of the next block). When i hits currentEnd you must jump again: jumps++, currentEnd = farthest. O(n) time, O(1) space.
explanation:
Same setup as Jump Game: nums[i] is the maximum jump length from index i, and you start at index 0. This time the last index is always reachable, and you return the MINIMUM number of jumps to get there. For [2, 3, 1, 1, 4] the answer is 2: jump 1 step to index 1, then 3 steps to the end.

"Fewest steps" usually means BFS (breadth-first search: explore everything one step away, then everything two steps away, and so on). Here every BFS level is a contiguous range of indexes, for the same reason as in Jump Game: if a jump can reach index 7 it can stop at 5 or 6 too. Level 0 is just index 0. Level 1 is every index from 1 up to nums[0]. Level k + 1 runs from the end of level k up to the farthest index any index in level k can reach. So you never need a queue, only two numbers.

Scan i from 0 to n - 2 (you never jump FROM the last index). Update farthest = max(farthest, i + nums[i]), the edge of the next level. When i == currentEnd you have looked at every index in the current level, so one more jump is needed: jumps++ and currentEnd = farthest. Return jumps.

The greedy part: within a level you don't decide WHICH index to jump from until you reach the level's end, and then you implicitly pick the one that reaches farthest. Any other choice reaches a subset of the indexes, so it can't need fewer jumps afterwards. Stopping the loop at n - 2 matters: with i running to n - 1, a scan that lands exactly on currentEnd at the last index would count one jump too many.

The visualization walks [2, 3, 1, 1, 4]. The highlighted cells are the level currently being scanned.

visualizationSteps.message: nums = [2, 3, 1, 1, 4]. Level 0 is just index 0 (zero jumps). currentEnd = 0, farthest = 0.
i = 0: farthest = 2. i has reached currentEnd = 0, the end of this level, so one more jump is needed. jumps = 1; the next level is indexes 1 to 2.
i = 1 is inside the current level (ends at 2). i + nums[i] = 4, so farthest = 4.
i = 2: farthest = 4. i has reached currentEnd = 2, the end of this level, so one more jump is needed. jumps = 2; the next level is indexes 3 to 4.
i = 3 is inside the current level (ends at 4). i + nums[i] = 4, so farthest = 4.
The last index lies inside the level reached with 2 jumps (it ends at 4). Answer: 2.

recognitionSignals: "Minimum number of jumps / steps / moves" on a line where each position allows a range of moves.
A BFS would work, but the levels are contiguous ranges, so two boundaries replace the queue.
The input guarantees the end is reachable (otherwise check reachability like Jump Game first).
gotchas: Loop to n - 2, not n - 1. Jumping from the last index is never needed, and including it can add an extra jump.
Update farthest BEFORE checking i == currentEnd, so the level boundary uses everything the level can reach.
confusableWith: Jump Game (this track) only asks whether the end is reachable, so one running maximum is enough.
Breadth-first search on a graph finds fewest steps in general; this is BFS where every level is an interval, which is what makes it O(1) space.
Dynamic programming (dp[i] = fewest jumps to reach i) is correct but O(n^2), because each index scans every earlier index.

complexity.note: BFS where every level is a contiguous range, so two boundaries (currentEnd, farthest) replace the queue; each index is scanned once.
